weeks.title: What data engineering actually is
weeks.context: Data engineering is the discipline of building the systems that move, store, and shape data so that analysts and ML models can trust it. Before you touch a single tool, you need the mental model: where data comes from, where it goes, and who depends on it downstream. This week you map the landscape and sketch your first pipeline on paper.

concept_check.q: Which responsibility most clearly belongs to a data engineer rather than an analyst?
choices: Building the pipeline that loads orders into the warehouse
concept_check.explain: Data engineers own the movement and shaping of data into reliable storage. Interpreting dashboards is analytics work, and building the app UI is software engineering. The pipeline that loads orders is squarely the engineer's deliverable.

concept_check.q: When is streaming the right choice over batch processing?
choices: When a daily summary email is enough
When fraud must be flagged within seconds of a payment
When cost must be minimised above all
concept_check.explain: Streaming earns its added complexity only when low latency is a real requirement, such as flagging fraud in seconds. Daily summaries and monthly data are classic batch cases. Streaming usually costs more, so it is not the cost-minimising default.

concept_check.q: Why must a production pipeline be idempotent?
choices: So a rerun does not duplicate or corrupt data
concept_check.explain: Reruns happen constantly in production after failures and backfills. An idempotent job yields the same result no matter how many times it runs, which prevents the double-counting that is the most common data bug. Speed and storage are unrelated to this property.

days.title: Data engineering vs analytics vs software engineering
days.summary: Focus: Data engineering vs analytics vs software engineering

items.title: Data engineering vs analytics vs software engineering
items.body:
## Data engineering vs analytics vs software engineering

Data engineers build the pipelines and storage that feed analysts and models; analysts query and interpret; software engineers build the apps that generate data in the first place.

## Why it matters
Knowing the boundary tells you what you own (reliable data delivery) versus what you consume or hand off.

## In practice
List the three roles and one deliverable each. A useful framing:

```text
Software eng  -> produces data (app events, orders)
Data eng      -> moves + shapes data (pipelines, warehouse)
Analyst/ML    -> consumes data (dashboards, models)
```

items.title: Deeper dive: Data engineering vs analytics vs software engineering
items.body:
## Deeper dive: Data engineering vs analytics vs software engineering

There isn't a single short video that nails this exact concept, so work it the way professionals actually learn it — by running small variations yourself and reading the output.

## Two more worked examples
1. Take the smallest case of **Data engineering vs analytics vs software engineering** and predict the result *before* you run it. Then run it and compare — the gap between your prediction and reality is the learning.
2. Change one variable (a column, a parameter, a condition) and predict again. Repeat until your predictions are reliably right.

## What to watch for
- Trace the data through each step (split, apply, combine) rather than memorising syntax.
- Read the shape and the index of every intermediate result; most bugs are shape bugs.
- When stuck, shrink the input to 3 rows you can verify by hand.

items.title: The data lifecycle: generation to consumption
items.body:
## The data lifecycle: generation to consumption

Data flows through generation, ingestion, storage, transformation, serving, and consumption. Each stage is a place something can break.

## Why it matters
If you can name the stage where a bug lives, you can fix it ten times faster.

## In practice
Trace one row of data end to end. The canonical lifecycle:

```text
generate -> ingest -> store -> transform -> serve -> consume
```

days.title: Batch vs streaming: the core trade-off
days.summary: Focus: Batch vs streaming: the core trade-off

items.title: Batch vs streaming: the core trade-off
items.body:
## Batch vs streaming: the core trade-off

Batch processing handles data in scheduled chunks (hourly, daily); streaming handles each event as it arrives (sub-second to seconds).

## Why it matters
Choosing wrong means either stale dashboards or wildly over-engineered infrastructure.

## In practice
Decide batch or streaming for three scenarios. A rule of thumb:

```text
Daily sales report      -> batch (cheap, simple)
Fraud alert on payment  -> streaming (latency matters)
Monthly payroll         -> batch
```

A typical stack today is: ingestion (Fivetran/Airbyte) -> warehouse (BigQuery/Snowflake) -> transformation (dbt) -> BI (Looker/Power BI), wired together by an orchestrator.

Almost every job description lists a subset of these; knowing the shape lets you read any architecture diagram.

## In practice

```text
sources -> ingestion -> warehouse/lake -> transform (dbt) -> BI
                                  \-> orchestration ties it together
```

```text
Platform eng  -> the warehouse + orchestration infra
```

days.title: Idempotency and why reruns must be safe
days.summary: Focus: Idempotency and why reruns must be safe

items.title: Idempotency and why reruns must be safe
items.body:
## Idempotency and why reruns must be safe

An idempotent pipeline produces the same result whether you run it once or five times; reruns are a daily reality, so non-idempotent jobs create duplicate or corrupted data.

## Why it matters
The single most common production data bug is a rerun that double-counts rows.

## In practice
Contrast a safe and an unsafe load. The pattern that saves you:

```sql
-- unsafe: appends duplicates on rerun
INSERT INTO sales SELECT * FROM staging;
-- safe: replace the partition
DELETE FROM sales WHERE dt = '2026-06-06';
INSERT INTO sales SELECT * FROM staging WHERE dt = '2026-06-06';
```

weeks.title: OLTP vs OLAP, star and snowflake schemas
weeks.context: Transactional databases (OLTP) and analytical databases (OLAP) are optimised for opposite goals. This week you learn why you never run analytics directly on the app database, and you model your first star schema: the backbone of every warehouse.

concept_check.q: Why should analytics queries not run directly on an OLTP database?
choices: Heavy scans contend with the app's fast writes and can degrade it
concept_check.explain: OLTP systems are tuned for many small concurrent writes that keep an app responsive. A long analytical scan competes for the same locks and resources and can slow or crash the application. That is why analytics belongs in a separate OLAP system.

concept_check.q: What does a fact table primarily store?
choices: Descriptive context like names and categories
Measurable events with foreign keys to dimensions
concept_check.explain: A fact table holds the measurable events of the business, such as a sale amount, along with foreign keys. The descriptive context lives in dimension tables. This separation is what lets you slice measures by any dimension.

concept_check.q: What problem does a Type 2 slowly changing dimension solve?
choices: It preserves historical attribute values when they change over time
It removes the need for keys
concept_check.explain: A Type 2 SCD keeps a new row each time a descriptive attribute changes, with valid-from and valid-to dates. This preserves history so reports about the past stay correct even after a customer moves or renames. It is about historical accuracy, not speed or compression.

## OLTP: systems built for writes

OLTP (online transaction processing) databases like Postgres and MySQL are tuned for many small, fast, concurrent writes that keep an application running.

## Why it matters
Running heavy analytics here will slow or crash the app your business depends on.

## In practice
Inspect a normalized OLTP shape. Typical rows are tiny and frequent:

```sql
INSERT INTO orders(user_id, total, created_at) VALUES (42, 19.99, now());
```

items.title: OLAP: systems built for reads at scale
items.body:
## OLAP: systems built for reads at scale

OLAP (online analytical processing) databases like BigQuery and Snowflake are tuned for scanning billions of rows for aggregates, using columnar storage.

## Why it matters
Columnar layout reads only the columns a query needs, which is why analytics queries fly here.

## In practice
Compare a scan query's home. OLAP shines at:

```sql
SELECT country, SUM(total) FROM orders GROUP BY country;
```

items.title: Normalization vs denormalization
items.body:
## Normalization vs denormalization

OLTP favours normalized tables (no duplicated data, many joins); OLAP often denormalizes to reduce joins and speed up scans.

## Why it matters
The right level of normalization depends entirely on whether you optimise for writes or for reads.

## In practice
Contrast the two shapes. Normalized splits; denormalized flattens:

```text
Normalized:   orders + users + products (3 tables, joins)
Denormalized: order_facts (1 wide table, no joins)
```

items.title: Facts and dimensions
items.body:
## Facts and dimensions

A fact table stores measurable events (a sale, a click) with foreign keys; dimension tables store the descriptive context (who, what, when, where).

## Why it matters
Separating facts from dimensions is what makes a warehouse queryable by business questions.

## In practice
Identify facts vs dimensions. A sale decomposes as:

```text
fact_sales: sale_id, date_key, product_key, customer_key, amount
dim_product, dim_customer, dim_date  (the context)
```

items.title: The star schema
items.body:
## The star schema

A star schema places one central fact table surrounded by denormalized dimension tables, joined by surrogate keys.

## Why it matters
It is the default analytical model because it balances query speed with understandability.

## In practice
Wire up a star. The join pattern:

```sql
SELECT d.month, SUM(f.amount)
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_date d ON f.date_key = d.date_key
GROUP BY d.month;
```

items.title: The snowflake schema
items.body:
## The snowflake schema

A snowflake schema normalizes dimensions into sub-dimensions (e.g., dim_product -> dim_category), trading some query speed for less redundancy.

## Why it matters
Knowing when to snowflake versus stay star keeps your model from becoming either bloated or slow.

## In practice
See the extra hop snowflaking adds:

```text
star:      fact -> dim_product(category_name)
snowflake: fact -> dim_product -> dim_category(category_name)
```

items.title: Surrogate keys and slowly changing dimensions
items.body:
## Surrogate keys and slowly changing dimensions

Surrogate keys are warehouse-generated integer keys that decouple the model from source IDs; slowly changing dimensions (SCD) track how descriptive attributes change over time.

## Why it matters
Without SCD handling, a customer who moves cities silently rewrites history in your reports.

## In practice
See a Type 2 SCD keep history with row versions:

```text
customer_key | customer_id | city     | valid_from | valid_to
1            | 42          | Banjul   | 2025-01-01 | 2026-05-31
2            | 42          | Serrekunda| 2026-06-01 | NULL
```

weeks.title: Data warehouses: BigQuery, Redshift, Snowflake
weeks.context: A cloud data warehouse is the analytical engine at the centre of the stack. This week you learn how columnar, distributed warehouses price and partition data, and you load your first dataset into one.

concept_check.q: What is the main architectural advantage of a cloud data warehouse?
choices: It separates cheap storage from elastic, on-demand compute
concept_check.explain: Cloud warehouses decouple storage from compute, so you store data cheaply and spin compute up only when querying. This lets spiky analytical workloads scale without permanent hardware. It is the defining property that makes terabyte queries affordable.

concept_check.q: On a per-byte-scanned warehouse like BigQuery on-demand, which habit saves the most money?
choices: Selecting only needed columns and filtering partitioned tables
concept_check.explain: When billing is per byte scanned, every unread column and partition you avoid is money saved. Selecting only needed columns and filtering on a partition key can cut scanned bytes dramatically. SELECT * does the opposite and inflates the bill.

concept_check.q: Why does partitioning a table by date reduce query cost?
choices: A date filter lets the engine skip partitions it does not need
concept_check.explain: Partitioning physically segments a table by a column such as date. A query that filters on that date only reads the matching partitions and skips the rest, cutting scanned data sharply. It is one of the highest-leverage warehouse optimisations.

items.title: Zero-cost path (free alternatives)
items.body:
## Zero-cost path (no credit card required)

This week mentions industry-standard tools that can cost money. You can complete every step for **free**, with no card and no trial that auto-renews:

- **AWS** — use **LocalStack** (mocks AWS APIs on your laptop) plus **MinIO** (local S3). The CLI commands are the same; set `--endpoint-url=http://localhost:4566`. No AWS account or card required.
- **Google Cloud / BigQuery** — use **DuckDB** (local, the same SQL, blazing fast) or local **Postgres**. No GCP account needed.
- **Cloud warehouse** — use **DuckDB** or local **Postgres**: identical SQL, zero cost.

Learn the concept with the free tool; the paid service is only how some teams run it in production. The skills and the code are the same.

items.title: What a cloud data warehouse is
items.body:
## What a cloud data warehouse is

A cloud warehouse separates storage from compute, stores data columnar and compressed, and scales query power on demand.

## Why it matters
Separation of storage and compute is why you can query a terabyte without owning a server farm.

## In practice
Note the architecture shift:

```text
old: one box holds data + compute (scaling = bigger box)
new: storage (cheap) <-> compute (elastic clusters)
```

items.title: BigQuery: serverless analytics
items.body:
## BigQuery: serverless analytics

BigQuery is fully serverless: you write SQL, Google manages the compute, and you pay per byte scanned or per slot-hour.

## Why it matters
Because you pay per byte scanned, SELECT * on a wide table is a literal money leak.

## In practice
Reduce bytes scanned by selecting only needed columns:

```sql
-- cheap: scans 2 columns
SELECT country, total FROM `proj.sales.orders`;
```

items.title: Snowflake: virtual warehouses
items.body:
## Snowflake: virtual warehouses

Snowflake separates storage from named virtual warehouses (compute clusters) that you size and auto-suspend independently.

## Why it matters
Auto-suspend means an idle warehouse stops billing within seconds, a key cost lever.

## In practice
Size compute to the job, not the data:

```sql
CREATE WAREHOUSE etl_wh WITH WAREHOUSE_SIZE='SMALL' AUTO_SUSPEND=60;
```

Redshift is AWS's warehouse built on provisioned node clusters with distribution and sort keys you choose explicitly.

Choosing the wrong distribution key forces network shuffles that dominate query time.

```sql
CREATE TABLE sales(...) DISTKEY(customer_id) SORTKEY(order_date);
```

items.title: Partitioning and clustering
items.body:
## Partitioning and clustering

Partitioning splits a table by a column (often date) so queries scan only relevant partitions; clustering co-locates similar rows to prune further.

## Why it matters
A date filter on a partitioned table can cut scanned bytes by 99 percent.

## In practice
Partition by date, cluster by a common filter:

```sql
CREATE TABLE events PARTITION BY DATE(ts) CLUSTER BY user_id AS SELECT ...;
```

items.title: Warehouse cost models
items.body:
## Warehouse cost models

Warehouses bill either per byte scanned (BigQuery on-demand) or per compute-time (Snowflake/Redshift), so the cheapest design depends on the pricing model.

## Why it matters
The same query can be cheap on one warehouse and expensive on another purely due to the billing model.

## In practice
Match optimisation to billing:

```text
per-byte  -> select fewer columns, partition, filter early
per-time  -> right-size compute, auto-suspend, cache results
```

Loading data means staging files (often in object storage), defining the target schema, and running a COPY/LOAD that the warehouse parallelises.

```sql
LOAD DATA INTO sales.orders FROM FILES (format='CSV', uris=['gs://bucket/orders*.csv']);
```

weeks.title: ELT vs ETL and dbt fundamentals
weeks.context: The industry shifted from ETL (transform before loading) to ELT (load raw, transform inside the warehouse). dbt is the tool that made ELT transformations testable, version-controlled software. This week you build your first dbt project.

concept_check.q: What fundamentally enabled the shift from ETL to ELT?
choices: Cheap, elastic warehouse compute that makes in-warehouse transforms practical
concept_check.explain: ELT loads raw data first and transforms inside the warehouse. This only became the default once warehouse compute turned cheap and elastic, removing the reason to transform on a separate box. The change is about economics of compute, not network speed.

concept_check.q: Why use ref() instead of a hard-coded table name in dbt?
choices: It builds dbt's dependency graph so models build in the right order
concept_check.explain: ref() tells dbt that one model depends on another, which lets dbt compute a build order and rebuild safely. Hard-coded names break that graph and can cause models to build before their inputs exist. The dependency graph is dbt's core value.

concept_check.q: What is the main benefit of dbt tests?
choices: They catch data-quality problems as failed builds before stakeholders see them
concept_check.explain: dbt tests assert expectations like uniqueness and non-null on your models. When data violates them the build fails, so you catch corruption early rather than after a wrong dashboard ships. They are about trust and early detection, not performance.

## In practice

```text
ETL: extract -> transform (external box) -> load
```

items.title: Sources and refs
items.body:
## Sources and refs

dbt sources declare raw input tables; ref() links models together so dbt can compute the correct build order automatically.

## Why it matters
Using ref() instead of hard-coded table names is what gives dbt its dependency graph and safe rebuilds.

## In practice
Reference an upstream model so dbt orders the build:

```sql
-- models/stg_orders.sql
SELECT * FROM {{ source('shop','orders') }}
-- models/fct_orders.sql
SELECT * FROM {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
```

items.body:
## Materializations

dbt models can be materialized as views, tables, incremental models, or ephemeral CTEs, trading freshness, cost, and speed.

## Why it matters
Choosing the right materialization is the difference between a 3-second and a 30-minute build.

## In practice
Set a materialization in config:

```sql
{{ config(materialized='incremental') }}
SELECT * FROM {{ ref('stg_events') }}
{% if is_incremental() %} WHERE ts > (SELECT max(ts) FROM {{ this }}) {% endif %}
```

weeks.title: Data lakes: S3, Delta Lake, Iceberg
weeks.context: A data lake stores raw and semi-structured data cheaply on object storage. Open table formats like Delta Lake and Iceberg add warehouse-like reliability on top. This week you learn file formats, partitioning, and the lakehouse pattern.

concept_check.q: Why does raw data typically land in object storage first?
choices: It is the only place SQL works
It is far cheaper and infinitely scalable for raw files
concept_check.explain: Object storage is cheap, durable, and scales without limits, making it ideal for landing large volumes of raw data. Warehouse storage costs more, so you stage raw files in the lake first. Schema enforcement is exactly what plain object storage lacks.

concept_check.q: What does Parquet provide that CSV does not?
choices: Columnar layout, compression, and explicit types
concept_check.explain: Parquet stores data by column with compression and typed schemas, so engines read only needed columns and files are far smaller. CSV is row-based, untyped, and bloated by comparison. Transactions come from table formats like Delta, not from Parquet itself.

concept_check.q: What core capability do Delta Lake and Iceberg add over plain Parquet files?
choices: ACID transactions and reliable table semantics over object storage
concept_check.explain: Delta and Iceberg layer a transaction log and metadata over Parquet, providing ACID guarantees, schema enforcement, and features like time travel. This turns a loose pile of files into a trustworthy table. Plain Parquet has no such transactional guarantees.

## Zero-cost path (no credit card required)

This week mentions industry-standard tools that can cost money. You can complete every step for **free**, with no card and no trial that auto-renews:

- **AWS** — use **LocalStack** (mocks AWS APIs on your laptop) plus **MinIO** (local S3). The CLI commands are the same; set `--endpoint-url=http://localhost:4566`. No AWS account or card required.
- **Google Cloud / BigQuery** — use **DuckDB** (local, the same SQL, blazing fast) or local **Postgres**. No GCP account needed.
- **Cloud warehouse** — use **DuckDB** or local **Postgres**: identical SQL, zero cost.
- **Azure** — substitute **LocalStack** / local tooling; the concepts transfer directly.

Learn the concept with the free tool; the paid service is only how some teams run it in production. The skills and the code are the same.

## Why Parquet beats CSV

Parquet is a columnar, compressed, typed file format; CSV is row-based, untyped, and bloated.

```python
df.to_parquet('orders.parquet')  # smaller + typed
```

items.title: The problem with raw lakes
items.body:
## The problem with raw lakes

Plain file lakes have no transactions, no schema enforcement, and no easy updates, leading to corrupt or half-written data (the data swamp).

## Why it matters
Without ACID guarantees, a failed write leaves readers seeing partial, inconsistent files.

## In practice
See the failure a naive lake allows:

```text
writer crashes mid-write -> readers see half a file -> bad results
```

items.title: Delta Lake: ACID on the lake
items.body:
## Delta Lake: ACID on the lake

Delta Lake adds a transaction log over Parquet files, giving ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and time travel.

## Why it matters
The transaction log is what turns a pile of files into something you can trust like a table.

## In practice
Write and time-travel a Delta table:

```python
df.write.format('delta').save('/lake/orders')
spark.read.format('delta').option('versionAsOf', 0).load('/lake/orders')
```

## Apache Iceberg and open formats

Iceberg is an open table format with hidden partitioning, schema evolution, and engine-agnostic metadata, increasingly the neutral standard.

## Why it matters
Open formats stop a single vendor from owning your data, since many engines can read the same tables.

## In practice
Note the portability promise:

```text
Iceberg table <- read by Spark, Trino, Flink, Snowflake, BigQuery
```

```text
object storage + Iceberg/Delta + query engine = lakehouse
```

weeks.title: Workflow orchestration: Airflow and Dagster
weeks.context: Orchestrators schedule, sequence, retry, and monitor the tasks that make up a pipeline. This week you learn DAGs, scheduling, retries, and the asset-based model, then build a small orchestrated pipeline.

concept_check.q: What is the main reason to use an orchestrator instead of cron?
choices: It manages task dependencies, retries, and visibility across many jobs
Orchestrators remove the need for code
concept_check.explain: Orchestrators run tasks in dependency order with retries, scheduling, and monitoring built in. Cron treats each job independently and fails silently, which collapses once jobs depend on each other. The value is coordination and visibility, not language support.

concept_check.q: In Airflow, what does the expression `extract >> load` mean?
choices: load runs only after extract succeeds
concept_check.explain: The >> operator sets a dependency so that load runs after extract completes successfully. It is how you express ordering in an Airflow DAG. The tasks are not merged or parallelised by this expression.

concept_check.q: How does Dagster's asset model differ from Airflow's task model?
choices: It centres on the data objects to produce rather than on tasks to run
concept_check.explain: Dagster models software-defined assets, meaning the tables and datasets you want to exist, and derives execution from them. Airflow centres on tasks and their order. The asset framing makes lineage and freshness first-class concerns.

items.title: Why orchestration exists
items.body:
## Why orchestration exists

An orchestrator runs tasks in dependency order, on a schedule, with retries and alerting, replacing fragile cron scripts.

## Why it matters
The moment you have more than two dependent jobs, cron and shell scripts become unmaintainable.

## In practice
Contrast cron with an orchestrator:

```text
cron: 3 independent jobs, no dependency awareness, silent failures
orchestrator: DAG with order, retries, visibility, alerts
```

items.title: Airflow DAGs
items.body:
## Airflow DAGs

In Airflow a DAG (directed acyclic graph) is Python code that defines tasks and their dependencies.

## Why it matters
Because the DAG is plain Python, your pipeline definition is testable, reviewable code.

## In practice
Define a two-task DAG with a dependency:

```python
extract = PythonOperator(task_id='extract', python_callable=do_extract)
load    = PythonOperator(task_id='load', python_callable=do_load)
extract >> load  # load runs after extract
```

items.title: Build a small orchestrated pipeline
items.body:
## Build a small orchestrated pipeline

weeks.title: Streaming basics: Kafka and Kinesis
weeks.context: Streaming systems process events the moment they occur. This week you learn topics, partitions, producers and consumers, delivery guarantees, and windowing, then publish and consume your first stream.

concept_check.q: What is a Kafka partition the unit of?
concept_check.explain: A topic is divided into partitions, which are consumed in parallel and preserve ordering within each partition. They are the fundamental scaling and ordering unit in Kafka. They are not about encryption or billing.

concept_check.q: Why does adding more consumers than partitions not raise throughput?
choices: Each partition is read by only one consumer in the group, so extras stay idle
concept_check.explain: Within a consumer group each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer. Once consumers equal partitions, additional consumers have nothing to read and sit idle. Throughput therefore scales with partition count, not raw consumer count.

concept_check.q: How do teams cheaply approximate exactly-once processing?
choices: By using at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers
concept_check.explain: True exactly-once is costly, so most systems choose at-least-once delivery and make consumers idempotent. Because reprocessing a duplicate has no harmful effect, the end result behaves as if exactly-once. At-most-once risks data loss and is rarely acceptable.

## Offsets and consumer groups

A consumer group splits a topic's partitions among members so the group scales horizontally while each partition is read once.

## Why it matters
Consumer groups are how you scale stream processing without double-processing events.

## In practice
Reason about group assignment:

```text
topic: 3 partitions, group of 3 consumers -> 1 partition each
add a 4th consumer -> it sits idle (no spare partition)
```

items.title: Delivery guarantees
items.body:
## Delivery guarantees

Streaming systems offer at-most-once, at-least-once, or exactly-once delivery, trading performance against duplicate risk.

## Why it matters
Most real systems use at-least-once plus idempotent consumers to approximate exactly-once cheaply.

## In practice
Compare the three guarantees:

```text
at-most-once : may lose events, never duplicates
at-least-once: never loses, may duplicate (dedupe downstream)
exactly-once : no loss, no dup (costlier)
```

weeks.title: Batch processing with Spark
weeks.context: Apache Spark is the workhorse for processing data too big for one machine. This week you learn its distributed architecture, DataFrame API, lazy evaluation, shuffles, and tuning, then run a real job.

concept_check.q: Why are Spark DataFrames usually preferred over RDDs?
choices: The Catalyst optimiser can rewrite DataFrame queries for speed
concept_check.explain: DataFrames expose a typed, declarative API that the Catalyst optimiser can analyse and rewrite into an efficient plan. RDDs are lower level and run exactly as written, missing those optimisations. So DataFrames are typically both shorter and faster.

concept_check.q: In Spark, when does a transformation like filter actually run?
choices: Only when an action such as count or write is called
concept_check.explain: Transformations are lazy: they build a logical plan but do not execute. Execution is triggered only when an action like count, collect, or write is invoked. This laziness lets Spark optimise the whole chain before running it.

concept_check.q: Why is a shuffle the operation you most want to minimise?
choices: It moves data across the network between partitions, which is expensive
concept_check.explain: Wide transformations such as joins and groupBy redistribute data across the cluster by key, sending it over the network. This network movement dominates runtime, so reducing shuffles is the heart of Spark tuning. Techniques like broadcast joins exist precisely to avoid it.

Transformations (select, filter, groupBy) are lazy and build a plan; actions (count, collect, write) trigger execution.

```python
orders.join(customers, 'customer_id')
```

items.title: Broadcast joins and tuning
items.body:
## Broadcast joins and tuning

Broadcasting a small table to every executor avoids shuffling the large table, a key tuning trick.

## Why it matters
A broadcast join can turn a 20-minute shuffle join into seconds when one side is small.

## In practice
Force a broadcast of the small side:

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
orders.join(broadcast(small_dim), 'product_id')
```

weeks.title: Data quality and testing
weeks.context: Data that is wrong but confident is worse than no data. This week you learn to assert expectations with dbt tests and Great Expectations, monitor freshness and anomalies, and gate pipelines in CI.

concept_check.q: Why is silently wrong data often worse than missing data?
choices: It propagates into trusted dashboards and erodes credibility unnoticed
concept_check.explain: Missing data is obvious and prompts investigation, but wrong data that looks fine flows into dashboards and decisions unchallenged. By the time it is discovered, trust in the whole data platform is damaged. That hidden propagation is what makes it more dangerous.

concept_check.q: What does a dbt relationships test assert?
choices: That every value exists as a key in a referenced table
concept_check.explain: A relationships test checks referential integrity: each value in a column must exist in the referenced table's key column. It catches orphaned facts that point to missing dimensions. It is about correctness of joins, not performance or encryption.

concept_check.q: Why run data tests in CI on every pull request?
choices: To block bad transformations before they reach production
concept_check.explain: Running tests in CI means a transformation that breaks an invariant fails the pull request and never merges. This shifts quality from a hope to an enforced gate. It is the same discipline software engineers apply to code, applied to data.

items.title: dbt tests as quality gates
items.body:
## dbt tests as quality gates

dbt's unique, not_null, accepted_values, and relationships tests assert table invariants on every build.

## Why it matters
Wiring tests into the build means corrupt data fails loudly instead of shipping silently.

## In practice
Assert a foreign-key relationship in YAML:

```yaml
columns:
  - name: customer_id
    tests:
      - relationships: {to: ref('dim_customer'), field: customer_id}
```

weeks.title: Data governance and cataloging
weeks.context: As data grows, people cannot find it, trust it, or know what is sensitive. Governance and catalogs solve discovery, lineage, classification, and access. This week you learn OpenMetadata, Amundsen, lineage, and PII handling.

concept_check.q: What is the primary purpose of a data catalog?
choices: To make data discoverable and trustworthy through searchable metadata
concept_check.explain: A catalog indexes tables, owners, descriptions, lineage, and usage so people can find and trust data. It is a search engine and documentation layer, not a storage or compute system. Its payoff is faster discovery and higher trust.

concept_check.q: What unique question does column-level lineage answer?
choices: Exactly which downstream columns a single source column feeds
concept_check.explain: Column-level lineage traces individual fields through transformations, so you can see precisely which outputs a given source column affects. Table-level lineage only shows table-to-table flow and misses that detail. This precision is vital for impact analysis and debugging.

concept_check.q: What does the principle of least privilege achieve?
choices: It limits the damage from mistakes and breaches by granting only needed access
concept_check.explain: Least privilege gives each role only the permissions it actually needs. If credentials are misused or leaked, the limited scope contains the blast radius. It is a core security control, distinct from performance or cost concerns.

items.title: Access control and least privilege
items.body:
## Access control and least privilege

Role-based access control grants the minimum permissions each role needs, and masking hides sensitive fields from those who do not.

## Why it matters
Least privilege limits the blast radius of both mistakes and breaches.

## In practice
Grant scoped, not blanket, access:

```sql
GRANT SELECT ON analytics.fct_orders TO ROLE analyst;  -- not GRANT ALL
```

concept_check.q: In 'ingestion layer: extract from source', what is the single most important thing to get right?
choices: Delivering the layer's goal reliably and idempotently
concept_check.explain: Each capstone week ships one reliable layer of the pipeline. The goal is correct, idempotent, documented output that the next layer can depend on. Chasing novel tools or volume of code misses the point of building a trustworthy system.

choices: Because shipping and versioning each layer makes the build reproducible and reviewable

concept_check.q: What makes the output of this week trustworthy for downstream layers?
choices: It is tested, idempotent, and documented so others can rely on it
concept_check.explain: Downstream layers can only build safely on output that is tested, safe to rerun, and documented. Those properties are what let a teammate or your future self depend on it without re-verifying everything. Size or visual polish do not create trust.

items.title: Handle pagination and rate limits
items.body:
## Handle pagination and rate limits

Loop through pages and back off on rate-limit responses to fetch complete data politely.

## Why it matters
Skipping pagination silently truncates your dataset; ignoring limits gets you blocked.

## In practice
Page until exhausted with backoff:

```python
while next_page:
    r = get(next_page)
    if r.status_code == 429: time.sleep(backoff); continue
    next_page = r.json().get('next')
```

items.title: Make extraction idempotent
items.body:
## Make extraction idempotent

Re-extracting a date should overwrite, not duplicate, that date's landing file.

## Why it matters
Idempotent extraction lets you safely rerun failed days during backfills.

## In practice
Overwrite the date partition deterministically:

```python
path = f'raw/dt={d}/data.json'  # same path each run for date d
```


items.title: Choose the file format
items.body:
## Choose the file format

Convert raw JSON/CSV landings to Parquet for cheap, typed, columnar storage.

## Why it matters
Parquet is the standard lake format because it slashes scan cost downstream.

## In practice
Convert a landing to Parquet:

```python
pd.read_json('raw/dt=2026-06-06/data.json').to_parquet('lake/trips/dt=2026-06-06/part.parquet')
```

items.title: Add an open table format
items.body:
## Add an open table format

Layer Delta or Iceberg over the Parquet files to gain ACID and time travel.

## Why it matters
A table format protects readers from half-written, partial files.

## In practice
Write as a Delta table instead of bare Parquet:

```python
df.write.format('delta').mode('append').save('lake/trips')
```

items.title: Make lake writes idempotent
items.body:
## Make lake writes idempotent

Overwriting a partition on rerun keeps the lake free of duplicates.

## Why it matters
Partition overwrite is the lake equivalent of the safe-rerun pattern.

## In practice
Overwrite just the affected partition:

```python
df.write.mode('overwrite').option('partitionOverwriteMode','dynamic').save('lake/trips')
```

items.title: Compact small files
items.body:
## Compact small files

Many tiny files slow reads; compaction merges them into right-sized files.

## Why it matters
The small-files problem quietly throttles every query until you compact.

## In practice
Reduce file count on write:

```python
df.repartition(1).write.parquet(path)  # fewer, larger files
```

Load lake Parquet into staging tables that mirror the source shape with minimal change.

Staging untouched data first keeps extraction and transformation cleanly separated.

```sql
LOAD DATA INTO capstone.stg_trips FROM FILES(format='PARQUET', uris=['gs://capstone-lake/trips/*']);
```

External tables query files in place; native loads copy data in for speed.

```text
external: query files in the lake directly (no copy)
native:   COPY into warehouse storage (faster scans)
```

items.title: Design the dimensional model
items.body:
## Design the dimensional model

Decide the fact grain and the dimensions needed to answer your question.

## Why it matters
Getting the fact grain right is the most important modelling decision you make.

## In practice
State the grain explicitly:

```text
fct_trips grain: one row per completed trip
dims: dim_station, dim_date, dim_weather
```

items.title: Deeper dive: Design the dimensional model
items.body:
## Deeper dive: Design the dimensional model

There isn't a single short video that nails this exact concept, so work it the way professionals actually learn it — by running small variations yourself and reading the output.

## Two more worked examples
1. Take the smallest case of **Design the dimensional model** and predict the result *before* you run it. Then run it and compare — the gap between your prediction and reality is the learning.
2. Change one variable (a column, a parameter, a condition) and predict again. Repeat until your predictions are reliably right.

## What to watch for
- Trace the data through each step (split, apply, combine) rather than memorising syntax.
- Read the shape and the index of every intermediate result; most bugs are shape bugs.
- When stuck, shrink the input to 3 rows you can verify by hand.

weeks.title: Orchestrating the pipeline
weeks.context: Wire ingestion, loading, and dbt into one scheduled, monitored pipeline.

concept_check.q: In 'orchestrating the pipeline', what is the single most important thing to get right?
choices: Delivering the layer's goal reliably and idempotently
concept_check.explain: Each capstone week ships one reliable layer of the pipeline. The goal is correct, idempotent, documented output that the next layer can depend on. Chasing novel tools or volume of code misses the point of building a trustworthy system.

concept_check.q: Why does this capstone week end with a 'ship' deliverable committed to the repo?
choices: Because shipping and versioning each layer makes the build reproducible and reviewable
concept_check.explain: Committing a working deliverable each week keeps the project reproducible and reviewable. It also means every layer is a stable foundation for the next. Shipping incrementally is how real data platforms are built and maintained.

concept_check.q: What makes the output of this week trustworthy for downstream layers?
choices: It is tested, idempotent, and documented so others can rely on it
concept_check.explain: Downstream layers can only build safely on output that is tested, safe to rerun, and documented. Those properties are what let a teammate or your future self depend on it without re-verifying everything. Size or visual polish do not create trust.

## What it is
Airflow / Dagster wired to the full pipeline is the foundation for this week's work. Without it installed and working, every later day will fail with a cryptic error.

## What you'll do today
- Install the required tool(s)
- Authenticate (if the tool talks to a cloud or remote service)

- Commit a `day0` checkpoint to GitHub

The #1 reason mentees stall is a missing CLI, a wrong PATH, or unauthenticated credentials. Spend 30 minutes here and save hours later.

weeks.title: Governance, catalog, and lineage
weeks.context: Document, classify, and expose lineage for the whole pipeline.

concept_check.q: In 'governance, catalog, and lineage', what is the single most important thing to get right?
choices: Delivering the layer's goal reliably and idempotently
concept_check.explain: Each capstone week ships one reliable layer of the pipeline. The goal is correct, idempotent, documented output that the next layer can depend on. Chasing novel tools or volume of code misses the point of building a trustworthy system.

concept_check.q: Why does this capstone week end with a 'ship' deliverable committed to the repo?
choices: Because shipping and versioning each layer makes the build reproducible and reviewable
concept_check.explain: Committing a working deliverable each week keeps the project reproducible and reviewable. It also means every layer is a stable foundation for the next. Shipping incrementally is how real data platforms are built and maintained.

concept_check.q: What makes the output of this week trustworthy for downstream layers?
choices: It is tested, idempotent, and documented so others can rely on it
concept_check.explain: Downstream layers can only build safely on output that is tested, safe to rerun, and documented. Those properties are what let a teammate or your future self depend on it without re-verifying everything. Size or visual polish do not create trust.

items.title: Set up your tooling
items.body:
## What it is
dbt docs + a data catalog for lineage is the foundation for this week's work. Without it installed and working, every later day will fail with a cryptic error.

## What you'll do today
- Install the required tool(s)
- Authenticate (if the tool talks to a cloud or remote service)
- Run a one-line verification command
- Commit a `day0` checkpoint to GitHub

## Why before anything else
The #1 reason mentees stall is a missing CLI, a wrong PATH, or unauthenticated credentials. Spend 30 minutes here and save hours later.

items.title: SQL in 100 Seconds
items.creator: Fireship
items.why: Chosen for clarity: this 2-minute Fireship explainer ('SQL in 100 Seconds') nails the core idea fast. Watch once, then do the exercise — the concept, not the syntax, is the point.

items.title: See it in action - the exact steps
items.body:
## Walkthrough
Do every step now, in your terminal.

```bash
pip install dbt-core
dbt --version
```

## What 'working' looks like
dbt prints version info.

If anything errors, read the message carefully - 90% of Day 0 failures are PATH or auth issues, both of which the error spells out.

## Context
This applies specifically to week 20 ('Governance, catalog, and lineage'), day 0.

items.title: Cost monitoring
items.body:
## Cost monitoring

Track warehouse and storage spend and attribute it to pipeline stages.

## Why it matters
Untracked cost is how a pipeline quietly becomes a budget problem.

## In practice
Watch spend by stage:

```text
warehouse bytes scanned + compute time + lake storage = daily cost
```

items.title: Deeper dive: Cost monitoring
items.body:
## Deeper dive: Cost monitoring

There isn't a single short video that nails this exact concept, so work it the way professionals actually learn it — by running small variations yourself and reading the output.

## Two more worked examples
1. Take the smallest case of **Cost monitoring** and predict the result *before* you run it. Then run it and compare — the gap between your prediction and reality is the learning.
2. Change one variable (a column, a parameter, a condition) and predict again. Repeat until your predictions are reliably right.

## What to watch for
- Trace the data through each step (split, apply, combine) rather than memorising syntax.
- Read the shape and the index of every intermediate result; most bugs are shape bugs.
- When stuck, shrink the input to 3 rows you can verify by hand.

Apply partition pruning, right-sized compute, and incremental builds to cut cost.

```sql
-- ensure dashboards filter on the partition column
WHERE dt BETWEEN @start AND @end
```

weeks.title: CI/CD and infrastructure as code
weeks.context: Automate testing and deployment of the pipeline and codify its infrastructure.

concept_check.q: In 'ci/cd and infrastructure as code', what is the single most important thing to get right?
choices: Delivering the layer's goal reliably and idempotently
concept_check.explain: Each capstone week ships one reliable layer of the pipeline. The goal is correct, idempotent, documented output that the next layer can depend on. Chasing novel tools or volume of code misses the point of building a trustworthy system.

concept_check.q: Why does this capstone week end with a 'ship' deliverable committed to the repo?
choices: Because shipping and versioning each layer makes the build reproducible and reviewable
concept_check.explain: Committing a working deliverable each week keeps the project reproducible and reviewable. It also means every layer is a stable foundation for the next. Shipping incrementally is how real data platforms are built and maintained.

concept_check.q: What makes the output of this week trustworthy for downstream layers?
choices: It is tested, idempotent, and documented so others can rely on it
concept_check.explain: Downstream layers can only build safely on output that is tested, safe to rerun, and documented. Those properties are what let a teammate or your future self depend on it without re-verifying everything. Size or visual polish do not create trust.

days.summary: Install and verify GitHub Actions CI/CD + Terraform before diving into the week.

items.title: Set up your tooling
items.body:
## What it is
GitHub Actions CI/CD + Terraform is the foundation for this week's work. Without it installed and working, every later day will fail with a cryptic error.

## What you'll do today
- Install the required tool(s)
- Authenticate (if the tool talks to a cloud or remote service)
- Run a one-line verification command
- Commit a `day0` checkpoint to GitHub

## Why before anything else
The #1 reason mentees stall is a missing CLI, a wrong PATH, or unauthenticated credentials. Spend 30 minutes here and save hours later.

items.title: See it in action - the exact steps
items.body:
## Walkthrough
Do every step now, in your terminal.

```bash
terraform -version
aws sts get-caller-identity
```

If anything errors, read the message carefully - 90% of Day 0 failures are PATH or auth issues, both of which the error spells out.

items.title: Manage secrets and config
items.body:
## Manage secrets and config

Keep credentials in a secret store and config in environment variables, never in git.

## Why it matters
A committed credential is a breach waiting to happen.

## In practice
Reference secrets, never inline them:

```bash
export WAREHOUSE_KEY=$(read from secret manager)
```

```text

```

items.title: Deeper dive: Write the README
items.body:
## Deeper dive: Write the README

There isn't a single short video that nails this exact concept, so work it the way professionals actually learn it — by running small variations yourself and reading the output.

## Two more worked examples
1. Take the smallest case of **Write the README** and predict the result *before* you run it. Then run it and compare — the gap between your prediction and reality is the learning.
